planting.note: Tuck nursery-grown plugs into gritty, sharply drained soil wedged into rock crevices or a scree bed in spring, mimicking the basalt cliff cracks where this plant naturally roots.

directions: This small tufted daisy is restricted to crevices and ledges on the basalt cliffs of the Columbia River Gorge, where it forms low cushions of narrow leaves topped by white-to-pale-lavender ray flowers with yellow centers in late spring to midsummer. It needs the same conditions it gets in the wild: lean, mineral soil with almost no organic matter, sharp drainage, and full sun with roots that stay dry between infrequent soakings. Because its native range is so narrow, treat it as a specialist rock-garden or crevice-garden subject rather than a general border perennial, and avoid any wild collection given its restricted distribution.

planting.note: Set container-grown plants into sharply drained, rocky or gravelly soil in spring, angling them into a slope or crevice so water sheds away from the crown through winter.

directions: Barrett's penstemon is a true basalt-cliff specialist of the Columbia River Gorge, trailing over rock faces and talus with waxy, leathery blue-green leaves and heavy spring displays of lavender-purple tubular flowers. It demands the excellent drainage of its native cliff habitat and resents any winter wet at the crown, so plant it on a slope, in a raised bed, or among rocks where water cannot pool. Once established it is quite drought tolerant and needs little summer water, making it a good choice for a dry rock garden well beyond its native Gorge range as long as drainage is sharp.

planting.note: Direct-sow fresh seed in fall into lean, rocky, well-drained soil where it will stay, since the long taproot resents transplanting once established.

directions: This desert parsley is a basalt-talus specialist of the Columbia River Gorge, forming a mound of finely dissected, blue-gray foliage beneath compound umbels of deep maroon-purple flowers that open in very early spring, well ahead of most garden perennials. It relies on a long taproot adapted to rocky, fast-draining slopes, so give it lean soil and avoid rich, moisture-retentive beds that invite rot. Once settled it needs very little supplemental water and provides one of the season's earliest nectar sources for native bees and other pollinators along the Gorge's dry basalt faces.

planting.note: Divide and plant clumps in fall into mossy, rocky, humus-flecked crevices with good drainage so they settle in before their very early spring bloom.

directions: Columbia kittentails grows on mossy basalt ledges and cliff faces of the Columbia River Gorge, forming a low rosette of rounded, toothed leaves topped by dense spikes of deep blue-purple flowers that open in late winter to earliest spring, among the first wildflowers to bloom along the Gorge. Plant it in a part-shaded crevice or ledge with gritty, well-drained but not bone-dry soil, since it grows naturally where moss holds a little moisture against the rock. It makes an excellent early-season accent for a native rock garden or shaded crevice planting, going dormant quietly through the heat of summer.

planting.note: Tuck rosette divisions into lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun, wedged among rocks the way the species naturally roots on open outcrops.

directions: Cascade stonecrop forms low, fleshy rosettes of gray-green succulent leaves on rocky outcrops, basalt ledges, and talus of the Columbia Gorge and adjacent Cascade foothills, distinct from the more common yellow-flowered Sedum oreganum found through much of the Pacific Northwest. In summer it sends up short clusters of creamy white, star-shaped flowers above the foliage before going into a drought-dormant rest. Give it the same lean, fast-draining, mineral soil and open exposure it gets on bare rock, since rich or constantly damp ground will rot the roots; it is well suited to a scree bed, trough, or crevice planting.
